record.title: SCOPE reports joint capability and safety post-training for computer-use agents
record.summary: An arXiv preprint presents SCOPE, a post-training recipe for computer-use agents that combines capability demonstrations, safe continuations around environmental hazards, explicit refusals and subsequent capability RL. On Qwen3.5-9B, the authors report 54.17% OSWorld task success and 64.30% OS-BLIND attack avoidance after RL, with a 58.80% harmonic mean in their benchmark setting. Matched-step ablations suggest refusal trajectories contribute most of the measured attack-avoidance gain, while safe-continuation trajectories better preserve task utility. These are author-reported results on one model and benchmark suite; OS-BLIND does not distinguish safe continuation from refusal or incidental task failure, and the aggregate is not a deployment safety guarantee.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report SCOPE joint post-training for Qwen3.5-9B using capability demonstrations, safe continuations and explicit refusals, followed by capability-oriented RL. SCOPE-RL reached 54.17% OSWorld task success and 64.30% OS-BLIND attack avoidance, with a 58.80% harmonic mean in the paper’s evaluation.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In matched-step SFT ablations, removing 81 explicit-refusal trajectories reduced OS-BLIND attack avoidance from 66.30% to 13.00%; replacing safe-continuation trajectories with additional refusals held attack avoidance at 66.70% but reduced OSWorld task success from 49.72% to 43.21%. The authors interpret refusal and risk-handling trajectories as serving different functions.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: OS-BLIND attack avoidance does not distinguish safe continuation from refusal or incidental task failure; the paper states its harmonic-mean aggregate is benchmark-specific and not a deployment safety guarantee.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction or inspection of the linked data/model artifacts was performed in this review.
OS-BLIND attack avoidance can count refusal or incidental failure as avoidance and does not by itself establish safe continuation; the aggregate score is not a deployment safety measure.
The reported training and benchmarks use Qwen3.5-9B and a bounded desktop GUI environment; generalization to other model families, applications and real user workflows is unknown.

brief.importance_rationale: If reproduced, the paper offers concrete evidence that explicit safety and risk-handling trajectories can alter computer-use behavior while capability RL recovers task success, a useful design choice for agent post-training. The result is limited to one model and benchmark suite, and its attack-avoidance metric does not distinguish safe completion from refusal or failure, so it does not establish deployment safety.
limitations: All reported model outcomes are author-reported and were not independently reproduced in this review.
The paper evaluates Qwen3.5-9B on OSWorld and OS-BLIND; transfer to other model families, applications and real user environments is unknown.
OS-BLIND attack avoidance does not distinguish safe continuation from refusal or incidental task failure.
The harmonic-mean capability–safety score is specific to the chosen benchmarks and is not a complete deployment safety guarantee.
Public linked artifacts were not inspected for availability, completeness or reproducibility.
brief.summary: An arXiv preprint presents SCOPE, a post-training recipe for computer-use agents that combines capability demonstrations, safe continuations around environmental hazards, explicit refusals and subsequent capability RL. On Qwen3.5-9B, the authors report 54.17% OSWorld task success and 64.30% OS-BLIND attack avoidance after RL, with a 58.80% harmonic mean in their benchmark setting. Matched-step ablations suggest refusal trajectories contribute most of the measured attack-avoidance gain, while safe-continuation trajectories better preserve task utility. These are author-reported results on one model and benchmark suite; OS-BLIND does not distinguish safe continuation from refusal or incidental task failure, and the aggregate is not a deployment safety guarantee.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report that joint capability–safety SFT followed by capability RL on Qwen3.5-9B yielded 54.17% OSWorld task success, 64.30% OS-BLIND attack avoidance and a 58.80% benchmark harmonic mean. Matched-step ablations show different effects from refusal and risk-handling trajectories.
technical.compute_or_cost: Training details include three SFT epochs and online RL across 64 concurrent environments; the paper does not report a deployment cost comparison or end-to-end serving economics.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint describes SCOPE methods, the SATraj-OS data composition and author-reported benchmark results. the research desk did not reproduce the training or evaluation.
technical.implementation_status: Experimental preprint with links to data/model collections; this review did not inspect those artifacts or verify deployment.
technical.mechanism: Generate programmatically verifiable GUI tasks, inject paired observable environmental risks without changing the user goal, train on capability/safe-continuation/refusal trajectories, then apply trajectory-balanced capability RL.
technical.novelty: Pairs capability tasks with safe variants and combines safe-continuation supervision with explicit refusal data before capability RL, distinguishing avoiding hazards while continuing from stopping harmful tasks.
technical.regime: Qwen3.5-9B evaluated on OSWorld and OS-BLIND. The released dataset table lists 2,740 retained trajectories from capability, environment-risk and refusal sources; online RL uses generated capability tasks.
technical.reproducibility: The paper links model and dataset resources and gives method/training details, but public artifact integrity and reproduction were not assessed here.
technical.strongest_baseline: The Qwen3.5-9B base, capability-only SFT and matched-step safety-trajectory ablations in the paper.

brief.title: SCOPE reports joint capability and safety post-training for computer-use agents
brief.why_it_matters: If reproduced, this work offers a concrete way to teach GUI agents both to avoid hazards while continuing benign work and to refuse harmful goals, then recover task execution through RL. The benchmark measures do not establish safe deployment: OS-BLIND avoidance conflates refusal and failure with safe continuation, and results cover one model family.
